title: Book 2, Chapter 6 — Beginning of the Peloponnesian War—First Invasion of Attica—Funeral Oration of Pericles
paragraphs: The war between the Athenians and the Peloponnesians and the allies on either side now truly begins. From this point all contact ceased except through heralds, and hostilities were started and carried on without a break. This history follows the order of events by summers and winters.

The thirty years’ truce that was made after the conquest of Euboea lasted fourteen years. In the fifteenth year, in the forty-eighth year of the priestess-ship of Chrysis at Argos, in the ephorate of Aenesias at Sparta, in the last month but two of the archonship of Pythodorus at Athens, and six months after the battle of Potidæa, just at the beginning of spring, a Theban force of a little over three hundred men entered Plataea under arms, about the first watch of the night. Plataea was a town of Boeotia in alliance with Athens. The Thebans were commanded by their Boeotarchs, Pythangelus, son of Phyleides, and Diemporus, son of Onetorides. A Plataean called Naucleides opened the gates to them. He and his party had invited them in, intending to put to death the citizens of the opposite party, bring the city over to Thebes, and so gain power for themselves. This was arranged through Eurymachus, son of Leontiades, a man of great influence at Thebes. For Plataea had always been at odds with Thebes, and the Thebans, foreseeing that war was near, wanted to surprise their old enemy in time of peace, before hostilities had actually broken out. This is also why they got in so easily without being noticed: no guard had been posted. When the soldiers had grounded arms in the market-place, the men who had invited them wanted them to set to work at once and go to the houses of their enemies. The Thebans, however, refused to do this. They decided instead to make a conciliatory proclamation and, if possible, to come to a friendly understanding with the citizens. Their herald therefore called on any who wished to return to their old place in the confederacy of their countrymen to ground arms with them, for they thought that in this way the city would readily join them.

When the Plataeans became aware that the Thebans were inside their gates and that the town had been suddenly occupied, they were alarmed. The night kept them from seeing the invaders, and they concluded that more had entered than was really the case. So they came to terms, accepted the proposal and made no move, especially since the Thebans offered violence to none of them. But somehow, during the negotiations, they discovered how few the Thebans were, and decided that they could easily attack and overpower them. The mass of the Plataeans were unwilling to revolt from Athens. At any rate they resolved to make the attempt. They dug through the party walls of the houses, and so joined one another without being seen in the streets. In the streets they placed wagons without the beasts, to serve as a barricade, and they arranged everything else as seemed convenient for the occasion. When they had done all that circumstances allowed, they watched their opportunity and went out of their houses against the enemy. It was still night, though daybreak was near. They reasoned that in daylight their attack would be met by men full of courage and on equal terms with their assailants, while in darkness it would fall on panic-stricken troops, who would also be at a disadvantage because the enemy knew the ground. So they made their assault at once and came to close quarters as quickly as they could.

The Thebans, finding themselves outwitted, immediately closed ranks to repel every attack. Two or three times they beat their assailants back. But the men shouted and charged them, while the women and slaves screamed and yelled from the houses and pelted them with stones and tiles. It had also been raining hard all night. So at last their courage gave way, and they turned and fled through the town. Most of the fugitives did not know the way out. This, together with the mud, the darkness (the moon being in her last quarter) and the fact that their pursuers knew the town and could easily cut off their escape, proved fatal to many. The only gate open was the one by which they had entered, and one of the Plataeans had shut it by driving the spike of a javelin into the bar in place of the bolt. So even here there was no longer any way out. They were now chased all over the town. Some climbed on the wall and threw themselves over, in most cases with fatal results. One party found a deserted gate, got an axe from a woman and cut through the bar; but they were soon seen, and only a few succeeded in getting out. Others were cut off in small groups in different parts of the city. The largest and most compact body rushed into a large building next to the city wall. The doors on the side of the street happened to be open, and the Thebans took them for the gates of the town and thought there was a passage right through to the outside. The Plataeans, seeing their enemies trapped, debated whether to set fire to the building and burn them just as they were, or whether there was something else they could do with them. In the end these men and the rest of the Theban survivors found wandering about the town agreed to surrender themselves and their arms to the Plataeans unconditionally.

While this was the fate of the party in Plataea, the rest of the Thebans were to have joined them with all their forces before daybreak, in case anything went wrong with the body that had entered. They received news of the affair on the road and pressed forward to help. Now Plataea is nearly eight miles from Thebes, and the rain that had fallen in the night delayed their march, for the river Asopus had risen and was not easy to cross. So they had to march in the rain and were held up at the river, and they arrived too late. They found the whole party either slain or captive. When they learned what had happened, they at once formed a design against the Plataeans outside the city. The attack had been made in time of peace and was perfectly unexpected, so there were naturally men and livestock in the fields. The Thebans wished, if possible, to take some prisoners to exchange for their countrymen in the town, should any chance to have been taken alive. Such was their plan. But the Plataeans suspected their intention almost before it was formed. Alarmed for their fellow citizens outside the town, they sent a herald to the Thebans. He reproached them for their unscrupulous attempt to seize the city in time of peace, and warned them against any outrage on those outside. If the warning were disregarded, the Plataeans threatened to put to death the men they had in their hands; but they added that if the Thebans withdrew from their territory, they would give the prisoners back to their friends. This is the Theban account of the matter, and they say that an oath was given them. The Plataeans, on the other hand, do not admit that they promised an immediate surrender, but say it depended on later negotiation; the oath they deny altogether. Be this as it may, the Thebans withdrew from their territory without doing any injury. The Plataeans then hastily brought in whatever they had in the country and immediately put the men to death. The prisoners numbered a hundred and eighty, and Eurymachus, the man with whom the traitors had negotiated, was one of them.

The Plataeans then sent a messenger to Athens, returned the dead to the Thebans under a truce, and set the city in order as the emergency seemed to require. The Athenians had been told of the affair right after it happened. At once they arrested every Boeotian in Attica, and they sent a herald to the Plataeans with an order not to proceed to extremes with their Theban prisoners until Athens had given instructions. Of course the news of the men’s death had not reached them. The first messenger had left Plataea just as the Thebans entered it, and the second just after their defeat and capture, so nothing later had come. The Athenians therefore gave their orders without knowing the facts, and when the herald arrived he found the men already dead. After this the Athenians marched to Plataea, brought in provisions and left a garrison there. They also removed the women and children and the men who were of least use.

With the treaty openly broken by the affair at Plataea, Athens prepared for war at once, and so did Lacedaemon and her allies. Both sides resolved to send embassies to the King and to any other barbarian powers from which either could hope for help, and both tried to win over the independent states at home. Lacedaemon gave orders to the states that had declared for her in Italy and Sicily. Besides the navy she already had, they were to build ships until the total reached five hundred, each city supplying a number fixed by its size, and they were also to furnish a stated sum of money. Until these preparations were complete, they were to stay neutral and receive Athenian ships in their harbors one at a time. Athens, for her part, took stock of her existing confederacy and sent embassies to the places nearest Peloponnese — Corcyra, Cephallenia, Acarnania and Zacynthus. She saw that if she could rely on these, she could carry the war all round Peloponnese.

That both sides cherished the boldest hopes and gave the war their utmost strength was only natural. Zeal is always greatest when an undertaking begins. This time both Peloponnese and Athens held many young men who had never seen war and were eager to take up arms, and the rest of Hellas watched in strained excitement as its two leading cities came into conflict. Predictions were recited everywhere, and oracles were chanted by the people who collect them, in the cities at war and elsewhere. Some time earlier there had also been an earthquake at Delos, the first in the memory of the Hellenes. It was said and believed to be an omen of what was coming, and nothing of the kind that happened was allowed to go unremarked. Men’s good wishes favored the Lacedaemonians strongly, all the more because they declared themselves the liberators of Hellas. Nothing that anyone could do for them, privately or publicly, by word or by action, was left undone. Each man felt that the cause was bound to suffer wherever he was not there to see to it himself. Such was the general anger against Athens, felt alike by those who wished to be free of her empire and by those who feared being swallowed up in it. With these preparations and these feelings the contest began.

The allies of the two belligerents were these. On the side of Lacedaemon stood all the Peloponnesians inside the Isthmus, except the Argives and Achaeans, who were neutral. Pellene alone among the Achaean cities joined the war at the start, though the others followed her later. Outside Peloponnese she had the Megarians, Locrians, Boeotians, Phocians, Ambraciots, Leucadians and Anactorians. Of these, the Corinthians, Megarians, Sicyonians, Pellenians, Eleans, Ambraciots and Leucadians supplied ships; the Boeotians, Phocians and Locrians supplied cavalry; and the other states sent infantry. This was the Lacedaemonian confederacy. The Athenian confederacy included the Chians, Lesbians, Plataeans, the Messenians in Naupactus, most of the Acarnanians, the Corcyraeans and the Zacynthians, together with tributary cities in these regions: coastal Caria and her Dorian neighbors, Ionia, the Hellespont, the Thracian towns, the islands lying to the east between Peloponnese and Crete, and all the Cyclades except Melos and Thera. Of these, Chios, Lesbos and Corcyra supplied ships, and the rest supplied infantry and money. Such were the allies of each party and their resources for the war.

Right after the affair at Plataea, Lacedaemon sent word around to the cities of Peloponnese and the rest of her confederacy, telling them to get troops ready, with the provisions needed for a campaign abroad, so as to invade Attica. Each state was ready by the appointed time and gathered at the Isthmus with two-thirds of its whole force. When the whole army had assembled, Archidamus, the Lacedaemonian king who led the expedition, called together the generals of all the states along with the principal men and the officers, and addressed them as follows:

“Peloponnesians and allies, our fathers fought many campaigns inside Peloponnese and beyond it, and the older men among us know war well. Yet we have never set out with a force larger than this one. If our numbers and our efficiency are remarkable, so is the power of the state we march against. We must not prove ourselves inferior to our ancestors, or unequal to our own reputation. All Hellas has fixed its hopes and its attention on this effort, and its sympathy is with the enemy of hated Athens. So, however large the invading army may look, and however sure some may be that our adversary will not meet us in the field, this gives no excuse at all for the least carelessness on the march. The officers and men of every city must always be ready for danger to arrive in their own quarter. No one can foresee the course of war, and its attacks are mostly decided by the impulse of the moment. Overweening self-confidence that despises preparation has often been withstood, though outnumbered, by a wise apprehension. Confidence is not out of place in an invading army; but in an enemy’s country it must go together with the precautions of apprehension. That combination best inspires troops to strike a blow and best protects them from receiving one. In this instance the city we are going against is far from helpless in defense; on the contrary, it is excellently equipped in every respect. We have every reason, then, to expect that the Athenians will take the field against us. If they have not set out already before we arrive, they will certainly do so when they see us in their territory, wasting and destroying their property. For men are always angered by injuries they are not used to suffering, especially when they are inflicted before their very eyes; and when they are least inclined to reflect, they rush most fiercely into action. The Athenians are the very people to do this above all others. They aspire to rule the rest of the world, and they are more accustomed to invading and ravaging their neighbors’ land than to seeing their own land treated in that way. Consider, then, the power of the state we are marching against, and the greatness of the reputation that, depending on the outcome, we shall win or lose for our ancestors and ourselves. As you follow wherever you are led, remember to hold discipline and vigilance as the first of duties, and to carry out the orders passed to you with alacrity. Nothing adds so much to the credit and safety of an army as large bodies of men united under a single discipline.”

With this brief speech Archidamus dismissed the assembly. His first act was to send Melesippus, son of Diacritus, a Spartan, to Athens, in case the Athenians, seeing the Peloponnesians actually on the march, might be more willing to submit. But they would not receive him in the city or in their assembly. Pericles had already carried a motion that no herald or embassy from the Lacedaemonians should be received once they had marched out.

So the herald was sent away without a hearing and ordered to be across the frontier that same day. In future, if those who had sent him wished to make a proposal, they must first go back to their own territory before sending embassies to Athens. An escort went with Melesippus to stop him from speaking with anyone. At the frontier, just as he was about to be dismissed, he said as he left: “This day will be the beginning of great misfortunes for the Hellenes.” When he reached the camp, Archidamus learned that the Athenians still had no intention of submitting, and only then did he begin his march and lead his army into their territory. In the meantime the Boeotians had sent their contingent and cavalry to join the Peloponnesian expedition, and with the rest of their forces they went to Plataea and laid waste the country.

While the Peloponnesians were still assembling at the Isthmus, or were on the march before invading Attica, Pericles, son of Xanthippus, one of the ten generals of the Athenians, saw that the invasion was coming. Archidamus happened to be his friend, and Pericles conceived that Archidamus might possibly pass over his estate and leave it unravaged. Archidamus might do so out of a personal wish to oblige him, or on instructions from Lacedaemon meant to set people against him, as had already been tried in the demand for the expulsion of the accursed family. So Pericles took a precaution. He declared in the assembly that, although Archidamus was his friend, the friendship would not be allowed to damage the state. If the enemy made an exception of his houses and lands and did not pillage them like the rest, he gave them up to the public at once, so that they could not bring him under suspicion. He also gave the citizens advice on their present affairs, in the same spirit as before. They should prepare for the war and bring their property in from the country. They should not go out to battle, but come into the city and guard it, and make ready their fleet, in which their real strength lay. They should also keep a tight rein on their allies. The strength of Athens came from the money that the allies’ payments brought in, and success in war depended chiefly on conduct and capital, so there was no reason for despair. Leaving other sources of income aside, the tribute of the allies brought in an average revenue of six hundred talents of silver. There were still six thousand talents of coined silver on the Acropolis, out of nine thousand seven hundred that had once been there; the money for the porch of the Acropolis, the other public buildings and Potidæa had been taken from this sum. This did not include the uncoined gold and silver in public and private offerings, the sacred vessels used in the processions and games, the Median spoils and similar resources, which amounted to five hundred talents. To this he added the treasures of the other temples, which were by no means small and could fairly be used. Indeed, if they were ever absolutely driven to it, they could take even the gold ornaments of Athene herself. The statue held forty talents of pure gold, and all of it could be removed. They could use this for their survival, but every penny of it must be restored. Such was their financial position, and surely it was a satisfactory one. Next, they had an army of thirteen thousand heavy infantry, besides sixteen thousand more in the garrisons and on duty at home in Athens. This was the number on guard at first, in the event of an invasion; it was made up of the oldest and youngest levies and of those resident aliens who had heavy armor. The Phaleric wall ran four miles before it joined the wall around the city. Of the wall around the city nearly five miles were guarded, though part of it was left without a guard, namely the part between the Long Wall and the Phaleric. Then there were the Long Walls to Piraeus, a distance of some four miles and a half, and the outer one was manned. Finally, the circumference of Piraeus together with Munychia was nearly seven miles and a half, but only half of it was guarded. Pericles also showed them that they had twelve hundred horse, counting mounted archers, sixteen hundred archers on foot, and three hundred galleys fit for service. These were the resources of Athens in each department when the Peloponnesian invasion was impending and hostilities were beginning. Pericles also urged his usual arguments for expecting a favorable outcome of the war.

The Athenians took his advice. They began to bring in their wives and children from the country, together with all their household goods, and even took down the woodwork of their houses. They sent their sheep and cattle across to Euboea and the nearby islands. But the move was hard for them, because most of them had always lived in the country.

This had been true of the Athenians more than of others since very early times. From Cecrops and the first kings down to the reign of Theseus, Attica had always been made up of a number of independent townships, each with its own town hall and magistrates. Unless danger threatened, nobody consulted the king at Athens. In ordinary times the townships ran their government and settled their affairs without his interference, and sometimes they even made war on him, as the Eleusinians did under Eumolpus against Erechtheus. In Theseus, however, they had a king as intelligent as he was powerful. Among the chief features of his reorganization of the country was the abolition of the council-chambers and magistrates of the small cities, which he merged into the single council-chamber and town hall of the present capital. Individuals could still enjoy their private property as before, but from then on they were obliged to have one political center only, Athens. She thus counted all the inhabitants of Attica as her citizens, and when Theseus died he left a great state behind him. From him, indeed, dates the Synoecia, or Feast of Union, which the state pays for and which the Athenians still keep in honor of the goddess. Before this the city consisted of the present citadel and the district beneath it, which lies rather to the south. This is shown by the fact that the temples of the other deities, apart from that of Athene, are in the citadel, and that even those outside it are mostly in this quarter of the city: the temples of the Olympian Zeus, of the Pythian Apollo, of Earth, and of Dionysus in the Marshes. It is in honor of this last that the older Dionysia are still celebrated in the month of Anthesterion, not only by the Athenians but by their Ionian descendants too. There are other ancient temples in this quarter as well. The fountain also was used in those days for the most important purposes, because it was so near. Since the tyrants altered it, it has been called Enneacrounos, or Nine Pipes, but when the spring was open it went by the name of Callirhoe, or Fairwater. Indeed, the old custom of using its water before marriage and for other sacred purposes is still kept up. Again, because they had once lived in that quarter, Athenians still call the citadel the city.

So for a long time the Athenians lived scattered over Attica in independent townships. Even after Theseus centralized the government, old habit remained strong. From early times down to the present war, most Athenians had gone on living in the country with their families and households. They were therefore not at all inclined to move now, especially since they had only just restored their establishments after the Median invasion. They were deeply troubled and discontented at giving up their houses and the hereditary temples of the ancient constitution, at having to change their way of life, and at saying farewell to what each of them regarded as his native city.

On arriving at Athens, a few of them had houses to go to, or could find refuge with friends or relatives. But the great majority had to make their homes in the parts of the city not built over, and in the temples and shrines of the heroes. The exceptions were the Acropolis, the temple of the Eleusinian Demeter and any other places that were always kept closed. The plot of ground below the citadel called the Pelasgian was forbidden to settlers by a curse, and there was also an ominous fragment of a Pythian oracle that said:
Leave the Pelasgian parcel desolate, Woe worth the day that men inhabit it!

Yet this too was now built over, because the moment demanded it. In my opinion, if the oracle came true, it did so in the opposite sense to what was expected. The misfortunes of the state did not come from the unlawful occupation; it was the war that made the occupation necessary. The god did not say so, but he foresaw that the day on which the plot came to be inhabited would be an evil day for Athens. Many people also lodged in the towers of the walls or wherever else they could. When all had come in, the city was too small to hold them, though later they divided the Long Walls and a large part of Piraeus into lots and settled there. Throughout this time great attention was being paid to the war. The allies were being mustered, and an armament of a hundred ships was being fitted out for Peloponnese. Such was the state of preparation at Athens.

Meanwhile the Peloponnesian army was advancing. The first town they reached in Attica was Oenoe, where they were to enter the country. They sat down before it and prepared to attack the wall with engines and other means. Oenoe lay on the border between Athens and Boeotia, and was of course a walled town; in time of war the Athenians used it as a fortress. So the Peloponnesians made ready to assault it, and they lost valuable time before the place. This delay earned Archidamus the severest criticism. Even while the war was being levied, he had been thought weak and favorable to Athens, because of the half measures he had urged. Once the army had assembled, his loitering at the Isthmus and the slow pace of the rest of the march had damaged his standing further. But all this counted for nothing beside the delay at Oenoe. During that interval the Athenians were bringing in their property, and the Peloponnesians believed that a quick advance would have found everything still outside, if he had not procrastinated. This was how the army felt toward Archidamus during the siege. But he, it is said, was expecting the Athenians to shrink from seeing their land wasted and to make their submission while it was still undamaged; and that was why he waited.

But after he had assaulted Oenoe, every possible attempt to take it failed, and no herald came from Athens. So at last he broke up his camp and invaded Attica. This was about eighty days after the Theban attempt on Plataea, right in the middle of summer, when the corn was ripe; Archidamus, son of Zeuxis, king of Lacedaemon, commanded. They encamped in Eleusis and the Thriasian plain and began their ravages. At a place called Rheiti, or the Brooks, they put some Athenian horse to flight. They then advanced, keeping Mount Aegaleus on their right, through Cropia, until they came to Acharnae, the largest of the Athenian demes or townships. There they sat down and formed a camp, and they continued their ravages for a long time.

Archidamus is said to have had the following reason for keeping his army in battle order at Acharnae during this incursion, instead of going down into the plain. He hoped that the Athenians, with so many young men and a standard of service never seen before, might be tempted to come out to battle and try to stop the devastation of their land. They had already met him at Eleusis and the Thriasian plain, so he tried whether the sight of a camp at Acharnae would provoke them to a sally. He considered the place a good position for a camp. He also thought it likely that the three thousand heavy infantry of the Acharnians, who formed so important a part of the state, would not submit to the ruin of their property and would force the rest of the citizens into battle. If, on the other hand, the Athenians did not take the field during this incursion, he could ravage the plain without fear in later invasions and advance right up to the walls of Athens. Having lost their own property, the Acharnians would be less willing to risk themselves for their neighbors’ property, and so there would be division in the Athenian counsels. These were the motives of Archidamus for staying at Acharnae.

Meanwhile, as long as the army was at Eleusis and the Thriasian plain, the Athenians still hoped it would come no nearer. They remembered that Pleistoanax, son of Pausanias, king of Lacedaemon, had invaded Attica with a Peloponnesian army fourteen years before, and had withdrawn without going beyond Eleusis and Thria. This retreat in fact caused his exile from Sparta, since he was thought to have been bribed to withdraw. But when they saw the army at Acharnae, barely seven miles from Athens, they lost all patience. The land of Athens was being ravaged before the very eyes of the Athenians. The young men had never seen such a sight, and the old had seen it only in the Median wars. It was naturally felt as a grievous insult, and everyone, the young men especially, was determined to go out and stop it. Groups formed in the streets and argued hotly; for if the proposed sally was warmly urged, it was in some quarters also opposed. Oracles of every kind of meaning were recited by the collectors, and each found eager listeners among one party or the other. The Acharnians were foremost in pressing for the sally, since they made up no small part of the army of the state and it was their land that was being ravaged. In short, the whole city was in a state of great excitement. Pericles was the object of general anger; his earlier counsels were entirely forgotten. He was abused for not leading out the army he commanded, and was held responsible for all the public suffering.

Meanwhile he saw that anger and infatuation were now in the ascendant, and he was convinced of the wisdom of his refusal to sally. He would not call an assembly or any meeting of the people, fearing the fatal results of a debate driven by passion and not by prudence. He devoted himself instead to the defense of the city and kept it as quiet as he could, although he constantly sent out cavalry to prevent raids by roving parties of the enemy on the lands near the city. There was a minor engagement at Phrygia between a squadron of the Athenian horse with the Thessalians and the Boeotian cavalry. The Athenians had somewhat the better of it until the heavy infantry advanced to support the Boeotians; then the Thessalians and Athenians were routed and lost a few men, whose bodies, however, were recovered the same day without a truce. The next day the Peloponnesians set up a trophy. The Thessalians came to the aid of Athens because of an ancient alliance; those who came were the Larisaeans, Pharsalians, Cranonians, Pyrasians, Gyrtonians, and Pheraeans. The Larisaean commanders were Polymedes and Aristonus, two party leaders in Larisa; the Pharsalian general was Menon; and each of the other cities had its own commander.

Meanwhile the Peloponnesians, since the Athenians did not come out to fight them, left Acharnae and ravaged some of the demes between Mount Parnes and Brilessus. While they were in Attica, the Athenians sent off the hundred ships they had been preparing to sail round Peloponnese, with a thousand heavy infantry and four hundred archers on board. The commanders were Carcinus, son of Xenotimus, Proteas, son of Epicles, and Socrates, son of Antigenes. This force set sail on its cruise. The Peloponnesians stayed in Attica as long as their provisions lasted, then withdrew through Boeotia by a different road from the one they had entered by. As they passed Oropus they ravaged the territory of Graea, which the Oropians hold from Athens; and on reaching Peloponnese they dispersed to their several cities.

After the Peloponnesians had gone, the Athenians posted guards by land and sea at the points where they intended to keep regular stations during the war. They also resolved to set apart a special fund of a thousand talents from the money in the Acropolis. This was not to be spent; the current expenses of the war were to be met from other sources. If anyone proposed or put to the vote a motion to use the money for any purpose whatever other than defending the city, in the event of the enemy bringing a fleet to attack by sea, the penalty would be death. With this sum they also set aside a special fleet of one hundred galleys, the best ships of each year, with their captains. None of these was to be used except with the money and against the same danger, should that danger arise.

The Athenians in the hundred ships round Peloponnese, meanwhile, received reinforcements: a Corcyraean squadron of fifty vessels and some other allies from those parts. They cruised along the coasts, ravaging the country, and among other places landed in Laconia and attacked Methone. The place had no garrison and its wall was weak. But Brasidas, son of Tellis, a Spartan, happened to be commanding a guard to defend the district. Hearing of the attack, he hurried to the help of the besieged with a hundred heavy infantry. The Athenian army was scattered over the country with its attention on the wall; he dashed straight through it and threw himself into Methone. He lost a few men forcing his way in, but he saved the place, and his exploit won him the thanks of Sparta. He was the first officer to be so noticed during the war. The Athenians at once weighed anchor and went on with their cruise. They put in at Pheia in Elis and ravaged the country for two days, and they defeated a picked force of three hundred men who had come to the rescue from the vale of Elis and the immediate neighborhood. Then a stiff squall struck them. They did not wish to face it where there was no harbor, so most of them boarded their ships, rounded Point Ichthys, and sailed into the port of Pheia. In the meantime the Messenians and some others who could not get on board marched across by land and took Pheia. The fleet later sailed round, picked them up, and put to sea; Pheia was abandoned, because the main army of the Eleans had now come up. The Athenians continued their cruise and ravaged other places on the coast.

At about the same time the Athenians sent out thirty ships, under the command of Cleopompus, son of Clinias, to cruise round Locris and to guard Euboea as well. He made landings from the fleet and ravaged some places on the coast. He captured Thronium and took hostages from it, and at Alope he defeated the Locrians who had assembled to resist him.

In the course of the summer the Athenians also drove the Aeginetans out of Aegina, together with their wives and children. Their reason was that the Aeginetans had been the chief agents in bringing the war upon them. Aegina also lies so close to Peloponnese that it seemed safer to hold it with colonists sent from Athens, and these settlers were sent out shortly afterwards. Lacedaemon gave the banished Aeginetans Thyrea as a refuge, partly because of her quarrel with Athens, and partly because the Aeginetans had put her under obligations at the time of the earthquake and the revolt of the Helots. Thyrea lies on the frontier of Argolis and Laconia, and its territory reaches down to the sea. The Aeginetans who did not settle there were scattered over the rest of Hellas.

In the same summer, at the beginning of a new lunar month (which, by the way, appears to be the only time it is possible), there was an eclipse of the sun after noon. The sun took the form of a crescent and some of the stars came out; then it returned to its natural shape.

In the same summer the Athenians appointed Nymphodorus, son of Pythes, an Abderite, as their proxenus, and summoned him to Athens. Sitalces had married his sister. Until then the Athenians had regarded him as their enemy; but he had great influence with Sitalces, and they wanted Sitalces to become their ally. Sitalces was the son of Teres and King of the Thracians. It was Teres, his father, who first established the great kingdom of the Odrysians on a scale unknown to the rest of Thrace, a large part of the Thracians being independent. This Teres has no connection with the Tereus who married Procne, the daughter of Pandion, from Athens; nor were the two from the same part of Thrace. Tereus lived in Daulis, in what is now called Phocis but was then inhabited by Thracians. In that land the women committed the outrage on Itys, and many poets, when they speak of the nightingale, call it the Daulian bird. Moreover, Pandion, when arranging an alliance for his daughter, would look to the benefits of mutual assistance, and would naturally prefer a marriage at that moderate distance to one that meant the many days of travel between Athens and the Odrysians. Again, the names are different; and this Teres was king of the Odrysians, the first, by the way, to gain any power. His son Sitalces was now being sought as an ally by the Athenians, who wanted his help in subduing the Thracian towns and Perdiccas. Nymphodorus came to Athens, concluded the alliance with Sitalces, and had Sitalces’ son Sadocus made an Athenian citizen. He promised to finish the war in Thrace by persuading Sitalces to send the Athenians a force of Thracian horse and targeteers. He also reconciled the Athenians with Perdiccas and got them to give Therme back to him; Perdiccas at once joined the Athenians and Phormio in an expedition against the Chalcidians. In this way Sitalces, son of Teres, King of the Thracians, and Perdiccas, son of Alexander, King of the Macedonians, became allies of Athens.

The Athenians in the hundred vessels, meanwhile, were still cruising round Peloponnese. They captured Sollium, a town of Corinth, and handed the city and its territory over to the Acarnanians of Palaira. Then they stormed Astacus, drove out its tyrant Evarchus, and brought the place into their confederacy. They next sailed to the island of Cephallenia and won it over without force. Cephallenia lies off Acarnania and Leucas and consists of four states: the Paleans, Cranians, Samaeans, and Pronaeans. Not long afterwards the fleet returned to Athens. Toward the autumn of this year the Athenians, under the command of Pericles, son of Xanthippus, invaded the Megarid with their whole levy, resident aliens included. The Athenians in the hundred ships round Peloponnese had just reached Aegina on the way home. They heard that the citizens were at Megara in full force, and they sailed over to join them. This was without doubt the largest army of Athenians ever assembled: the state was still in the flower of her strength and had not yet been visited by the plague. There were fully ten thousand heavy infantry in the field, all Athenian citizens, not counting the three thousand before Potidæa. The resident aliens who joined the invasion numbered at least three thousand, and there was also a multitude of light troops. They ravaged most of the territory and then withdrew. The Athenians afterwards invaded the Megarid again every year during the war, sometimes with cavalry only, sometimes with all their forces, until Nisaea was captured. Toward the end of this summer the Athenians also turned Atalanta, the desert island off the Opuntian coast, into a fortified post, to stop privateers from Opus and the rest of Locris from sailing out and plundering Euboea. These were the events of the summer after the Peloponnesians returned from Attica.

The next winter the Acarnanian Evarchus, who wished to return to Astacus, persuaded the Corinthians to sail over and restore him with forty ships and fifteen hundred heavy infantry; he also hired some mercenaries of his own. Euphamidas, son of Aristonymus, Timoxenus, son of Timocrates, and Eumachus, son of Chrysis, were in command. They sailed over and restored him. They then tried to gain some places on the Acarnanian coast, failed, and began the voyage home. Coasting along the shore, they put in at Cephallenia and landed in Cranian territory. The Cranians agreed to negotiate and then fell suddenly upon them, killing some of their men; the Corinthians put to sea in some haste and returned home.

In the same winter the Athenians gave a public funeral to the first men who had fallen in this war. The custom is an ancestral one, and the procedure is as follows. The bones of the dead are laid out in a tent set up for the purpose, three days before the ceremony, and friends bring their relatives whatever offerings they wish. When the procession takes place, cypress coffins are carried on carts, one for each tribe, and the bones of each man go into the coffin of his tribe. One empty bier, decked out for the missing, is carried along with them; these are the men whose bodies could not be recovered. Any citizen or stranger who wishes may join the procession, and the women of the families attend to wail at the grave. The dead are laid in the public sepulchre, in the Beautiful suburb of the city, where those who fall in war are always buried. The exception is the men who were killed at Marathon: for their singular and extraordinary valor they were buried on the spot where they fell. When the bodies have been covered with earth, a man chosen by the state for his approved wisdom and eminent reputation delivers a fitting panegyric over them, and then all depart. This is how burials are conducted; and throughout the war the established custom was observed whenever the occasion arose. These men were the first to fall, and Pericles, son of Xanthippus, was chosen to deliver their eulogy. When the time came, he moved forward from the sepulchre onto a raised platform, so that as many of the crowd as possible could hear him, and spoke as follows:

“Most of my predecessors in this place have praised the man who added this speech to the law, saying that it is right for it to be delivered at the burial of those who fall in battle. For myself, I would have thought that men whose worth showed itself in deeds would be sufficiently rewarded by honors also shown in deeds, such as you now see in this funeral prepared at the people’s expense. And I could have wished that the reputations of many brave men were not put at risk in the mouth of a single speaker, to stand or fall according as he speaks well or ill. For it is hard to speak properly on a subject where it is even difficult to convince your hearers that you are speaking the truth. The friend who knows every fact of the story may think that some point has not been set out as fully as he wishes and knows it deserves; the stranger to the matter, on the other hand, may be led by envy to suspect exaggeration if he hears anything beyond his own capacity. For men can bear to hear others praised only so long as each can persuade himself that he could equal the actions described. Once that point is passed, envy comes in, and with it disbelief. However, since our ancestors approved this custom, it is my duty to obey the law and to try to satisfy your several wishes and opinions as well as I can.

“I shall begin with our ancestors, since it is both just and proper that they should have the honor of first mention on an occasion like this. They lived in the country without interruption, generation after generation, and by their valor handed it down free to the present day. If our more remote ancestors deserve praise, our own fathers deserve much more. To their inheritance they added the empire we now possess, and they spared no pains to leave their acquisitions to us of the present generation. And there are few parts of our dominions that have not been enlarged by those of us here who are still more or less in the vigor of life, while we have furnished the mother country with everything she needs to depend on her own resources in war or in peace. The military achievements by which we gained our several possessions, and the ready valor with which either we or our fathers stemmed the tide of Hellenic or foreign aggression, are a theme too familiar to my hearers for me to dwell on, and I shall therefore pass it by. But by what road we reached our position, under what form of government our greatness grew, and out of what national habits it sprang: these are questions I may try to answer before I proceed to my panegyric upon these men. I think this a subject on which a speaker may properly dwell on the present occasion, and one that the whole assembly, citizens and foreigners alike, may listen to with advantage.

“Our constitution does not copy the laws of our neighbors. We are a pattern to others rather than imitators of them. Our administration favors the many instead of the few, and that is why it is called a democracy. In private disputes the laws give equal justice to all. As for social standing, advancement in public life goes to reputation for capacity, and class considerations are not allowed to interfere with merit. Nor does poverty bar the way: a man who can serve the state is not hindered by the obscurity of his condition. The freedom we enjoy in public life extends also to our ordinary life. In that, far from keeping a jealous watch on one another, we do not feel called upon to be angry with a neighbor for doing as he likes, or even to give him those injurious looks which cannot fail to give offense, though they inflict no actual penalty. But this ease in our private relations does not make us lawless as citizens. Fear is our chief safeguard against that. It teaches us to obey the magistrates and the laws, above all those that protect the injured, whether they are actually on the statute book or belong to the unwritten code that cannot be broken without acknowledged disgrace.

“We also provide plenty of ways for the mind to refresh itself after business. We celebrate games and sacrifices all the year round, and the elegance of our private establishments gives daily pleasure and helps to banish gloom. And because our city is so large, the produce of the whole world is drawn into our harbor, so that the Athenian enjoys the fruits of other countries as familiarly as those of his own.

“If we turn to our military policy, there too we differ from our opponents. We throw open our city to the world and never, by laws against aliens, exclude foreigners from any opportunity of learning or observing, although an enemy’s eyes may occasionally profit by our liberality. We trust less in system and policy than in the native spirit of our citizens. And in education, where our rivals seek manliness from the cradle by painful discipline, at Athens we live exactly as we please, and yet are just as ready to face every legitimate danger. As proof of this, the Lacedaemonians do not invade our country alone but bring all their confederates with them, while we Athenians advance unsupported into a neighbor’s territory and, fighting on foreign soil, usually defeat with ease men who are defending their homes. Our united force has never yet been met by any enemy, because we have at once to attend to our navy and to send our citizens by land on a hundred different services. So wherever the enemy engage some such fraction of our strength, a success against a detachment is magnified into a victory over the whole nation, and a defeat into a reverse suffered at the hands of our entire people. And yet if we are still willing to face danger with habits of ease rather than labor, and with courage that comes from nature rather than art, we have the double advantage of not suffering hardships in anticipation, and of meeting them in the hour of need as fearlessly as those who are never free from them.

“These are not the only points in which our city deserves admiration. We cultivate refinement without extravagance and knowledge without softness. We employ wealth more for use than for show, and we think the real disgrace of poverty lies not in admitting to it but in not struggling against it. Our public men also have private affairs to attend to, and our ordinary citizens, though busy with their trades, are still fair judges of public matters. We are unlike any other nation in this: we regard a man who takes no part in these duties as useless, not as unambitious. We Athenians can at all events judge a proposal, even if we cannot originate one; and we do not see discussion as a stumbling-block in the way of action. We think it an indispensable preliminary to any wise action at all. In our enterprises, again, we present the singular spectacle of daring and deliberation, each carried to its highest point and both united in the same persons, although decision is usually the fruit of ignorance, and hesitation of reflection. But the palm of courage will surely be awarded most justly to those who know best the difference between hardship and pleasure and yet are never tempted to shrink from danger. In generosity, too, we are singular, since we win our friends by conferring favors, not by receiving them. Yet of course the giver of a favor is the firmer friend of the two, wishing by continued kindness to keep the recipient in his debt. The debtor feels less keenly, because he knows that his return will be a payment, not a free gift. And only the Athenians, fearless of consequences, confer their benefits not out of calculations of expediency but in the confidence of liberality.

“In short, I say that as a city we are the school of Hellas, and I doubt whether the world can produce a man who, depending only on himself, is equal to so many emergencies and has so happy a versatility as the Athenian. That this is no mere boast made for the occasion but plain matter of fact is proved by the power the state has acquired through these habits. Athens alone of her contemporaries is found, when tested, to be greater than her reputation. She alone gives her assailants no cause to blush at the antagonist by whom they have been worsted, and gives her subjects no cause to question her title to rule by merit. Rather, we shall have the admiration of the present and of later ages, since we have not left our power without witness but have shown it by mighty proofs. Far from needing a Homer to praise us, or any other of his craft whose verses might charm for the moment but whose impression would melt at the touch of fact, we have forced every sea and land to be the highway of our daring, and everywhere, for evil or for good, we have left imperishable monuments behind us. Such is the Athens for which these men nobly fought and died, asserting their resolve not to lose her; and well may every one of their survivors be ready to suffer in her cause.

“If I have dwelt at some length on the character of our country, it was to show that we have more at stake in this struggle than men who have no such blessings to lose, and at the same time to establish by definite proofs the panegyric of the men over whom I am now speaking. That panegyric is now largely complete. The Athens I have celebrated is only what the heroism of these men and their like has made her; and their fame, unlike that of most Hellenes, will be found to match their deserts exactly. If a test of worth is wanted, it lies in the way they ended their lives. This holds not only where that ending set the final seal on a man’s merit, but also where it gave the first sign that he had any. For it is just to claim that steadfastness in his country’s battles should cover a man’s other imperfections like a cloak: the good action has blotted out the bad, and his merit as a citizen has more than outweighed his faults as an individual. Yet none of these men let wealth, with its prospect of future enjoyment, unnerve his spirit, or let poverty, with its hope of a day of freedom and riches, tempt him to shrink from danger. No: they held vengeance upon their enemies to be more desirable than any personal blessing, and reckoned it the most glorious of hazards. So they joyfully chose to accept the risk, to make sure of their vengeance, and to let their wishes wait. They committed to hope the uncertainty of final success, but in the business before them they thought it right to act boldly and trust in themselves. Choosing to die resisting rather than to live submitting, they fled only from dishonor, but met danger face to face; and after one brief moment, at the summit of their fortune, they escaped, not from their fear, but from their glory.

“So died these men, as became Athenians. You, their survivors, must resolve to have as unfaltering a spirit in the field, though you may pray for a happier outcome. Do not be content with ideas drawn only from words about the advantages of defending your country. A speaker could make a valuable text of these even before an audience as alive to them as this one. You must yourselves realize the power of Athens and feed your eyes upon her from day to day, until love of her fills your hearts. Then, when all her greatness has broken upon you, reflect that men won it by courage, a sense of duty, and a keen feeling of honor in action. Reflect too that when they failed in some enterprise, they would not consent to deprive their country of their valor, but laid it at her feet as the most glorious contribution they could offer. All of them gave their lives in common, and each of them received individually that renown which never grows old. They received also a sepulchre: not so much the one where their bones lie, as that noblest of shrines in which their glory is stored up, to be remembered forever whenever deed or story calls for its commemoration. For heroes have the whole earth for their tomb. In lands far from their own, where the column with its epitaph declares it, there is enshrined in every breast an unwritten record, with no tablet to preserve it except that of the heart. Take these men as your model. Judge happiness to be the fruit of freedom, and freedom of valor, and never decline the dangers of war. For it is not the wretched, who have nothing to hope for, who would most justly be unsparing of their lives. It is rather those to whom continued life may bring reverses as yet unknown, and for whom a fall, if it came, would have the most tremendous consequences. And surely, to a man of spirit, the degradation of cowardice is immeasurably more grievous than the unfelt death that strikes him in the midst of his strength and patriotism!

“Comfort, therefore, not condolence, is what I have to offer to those parents of the dead who are here. They know that life is subject to numberless chances; but fortunate are those who draw as their lot a death as glorious as the one that has caused your mourning, and whose lives have been measured so exactly that they end in the happiness in which they were spent. Still, I know this is a hard saying, especially since you will constantly be reminded of the dead when you see in other people’s homes the blessings in which you once took pride. For grief is felt not so much for the want of what we have never known as for the loss of what we have long been used to. Yet you who are still of an age to have children must bear up in the hope of having others in their place. They will help you to forget those you have lost, and they will be to the state both a reinforcement and a security; for no fair or just policy can be expected from a citizen who does not, like his fellows, bring a father’s interests and apprehensions to the decision. As for those of you who are past your prime, you must count it a gain that the best part of your life was fortunate, and that the short span that remains will be cheered by the fame of the departed. For only the love of honor never grows old; and what rejoices the heart of age and helplessness is honor, not gain, as some would have it.

“To the sons or brothers of the dead I turn next, and I see a hard struggle before you. When a man is gone, everyone is accustomed to praise him. However transcendent your merit, you will find it difficult not only to overtake their renown but even to come near it. The living have envy to contend with, while those who are no longer in our path are honored with a goodwill that rivalry does not touch. And if I must say something on the subject of female excellence to those of you who will now be widows, one short exhortation will contain it all. Great will be your glory if you do not fall short of your natural character, and greatest will be the glory of the woman who is least talked of among the men, whether for good or for bad.

“My task is now finished. I have performed it as well as I could, and as far as words go, the requirements of the law are satisfied. As for deeds, those who lie buried here have already received part of their honors, and the rest they will receive through their children, who will be brought up at public expense until they are grown. In this way the state offers a valuable prize, like the garland of victory in this race of valor, both to those who have fallen and to their survivors. And where the rewards for merit are greatest, there the best citizens are found.
“Now that you have finished lamenting your relatives, you may depart.”
